title: MCP authorization: OAuth 2.1, PRM, CIMD vs DCR
summary: A protected MCP server is an OAuth 2.1 resource server. Clients find its authorization server through protected resource metadata, register with a client ID metadata document, run authorization code with PKCE and send an audience-bound token on every request.
useIf: You expose or consume a remote MCP server that must know which user or application is calling.
avoidIf: The server is a local stdio process. The spec says stdio servers SHOULD NOT follow this flow and should read credentials from the environment.

explain.md: Authorization is optional. When an HTTP server uses it, the MCP server acts as an **OAuth 2.1 resource server** and the client as an OAuth 2.1 client. The spec cites the IETF draft `draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-13`, not a published RFC, plus RFC 8414, RFC 8707, RFC 9728 and RFC 9207 [[r4]].

explain.title: Discovery and token flow
explain.alt: The client calls the MCP server without a token and gets 401 with resource_metadata. It reads protected resource metadata, fetches authorization server metadata, authorizes with PKCE and the resource parameter, then calls the server with a bearer token.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant M as MCP server
  participant A as Auth server
  C->>M: request, no token
  M-->>C: 401 resource_metadata
  C->>M: GET protected resource metadata
  M-->>C: authorization_servers
  C->>A: GET server metadata
  C->>A: authorize with PKCE S256 and resource
  A-->>C: access token
  C->>M: request, Authorization Bearer

explain.md: **Discovery.** Servers MUST implement RFC 9728 protected resource metadata with at least one `authorization_servers` entry. They advertise it with `resource_metadata` in the 401 `WWW-Authenticate` header or at `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`, and clients MUST support both. Authorization servers need RFC 8414 or OpenID Connect Discovery metadata [[tr10]] [[tr17]].

**Rules that matter.** Clients MUST use PKCE with `S256` and refuse to proceed if `code_challenge_methods_supported` is absent. Redirect URIs MUST be `localhost` or HTTPS and matched exactly. Clients MUST send the RFC 8707 `resource` parameter (the canonical server URI) in authorization and token requests, and servers MUST validate that tokens were issued for them [[r34]] [[tr18]]. Authorization servers SHOULD return `iss` (RFC 9207) and clients MUST compare it exactly before redeeming the code [[tr20]]. A 403 with `insufficient_scope` triggers step-up, and clients treat the challenged scopes as authoritative.

explain.title: Entra ID
explain.md: With Entra the server is the protected resource and Entra is the authorization server. Entra matches `resource` to the app registration's Application ID URI, and the app must request v2 tokens (`requestedAccessTokenVersion: 2`). Whether Entra supports DCR or CIMD for arbitrary MCP clients is UNVERIFIED as of 2026-10-13, so assume pre-registration [[r18]].

whereToUse: A remote SaaS server that acts on behalf of each user
An internal server fronted by Entra ID or another enterprise IdP
Hosts that connect to many third-party servers and must register with each authorization server
Machine-to-machine servers using the client credentials extension

use: Use per-user OAuth when a person is present and actions need their identity
Use CIMD when the authorization server supports it and clients are not pre-registered
Use pre-registered credentials when you control both sides
Use the opt-in extensions for machine or enterprise-managed access
avoid: Applying this flow to stdio servers
Accepting tokens whose audience is not your server
Writing token validation yourself where your IdP provides it
flips: No user is present: use the client credentials extension
A central IdP must decide which servers staff can reach: use enterprise-managed authorization

pitfalls.cause: The server lacks protected resource metadata or `resource_metadata` in the challenge
pitfalls.fix: Serve RFC 9728 metadata at the well-known path and in `WWW-Authenticate`

pitfalls.symptom: Token requests are rejected or tokens carry the wrong audience
pitfalls.cause: The `resource` value does not match the server's canonical URI or app registration
pitfalls.fix: Use the canonical URI consistently and, on Entra, request v2 tokens

pitfalls.symptom: Registrations pile up at the authorization server
pitfalls.fix: Prefer CIMD or pre-registration, and reuse credentials bound to that authorization server

scenarios.title: A desktop host meeting unknown remote servers
scenarios.situation: A desktop assistant lets users add any remote MCP server. Each server has its own authorization server. A person is present for every sign-in.
constraints: Public client, cannot keep a secret
unknowns: Does the authorization server advertise CIMD support?
What trust policy applies to client metadata URLs?
scenarios.question: How should the client identify itself?

options.name: Client ID Metadata Document, with DCR as a fallback
options.why: It follows the spec's registration order and avoids a registration per run.
options.tradeoff: You host a metadata document and authorization servers must trust the URL.

options.name: Dynamic Client Registration only
options.why: Widely available and works where CIMD does not.
options.tradeoff: It is Deprecated and creates registration records on every server.

options.name: One shared client ID and secret embedded in the app
options.why: A public client cannot protect a secret and every user shares one identity.
options.tradeoff: Pre-registered credentials are right when you control the servers.

flips.if: You operate both client and servers
The authorization server supports neither CIMD nor DCR
flips.then: Ask the user for credentials supplied by the server owner.

scenarios.takeaway: Try pre-registration, then CIMD, then DCR.

scenarios.title: A nightly agent with no user
scenarios.situation: A scheduled agent calls an internal MCP server at 2 a.m. to export reports. No person can approve a browser prompt.
unknowns: Does the client support the client credentials extension?
What scopes should the machine identity hold?
scenarios.question: How does the agent authenticate?

options.name: Client credentials extension with a scoped machine identity
options.why: Built for machine to machine access and needs no interactive consent.
options.tradeoff: Opt-in extension, so client and server support must be confirmed.

options.name: A subscription key checked at a gateway
options.tradeoff: Weaker identity and rotation story than OAuth tokens.

options.name: Authorization code flow with a browser
options.why: Nobody is present to complete it.
options.tradeoff: Right when a user is present.

flips.if: The export must run as a specific user
flips.then: Use delegated tokens with a stored refresh token under strict controls.
Use the gateway key until support arrives.

scenarios.takeaway: No user means a machine flow, not a browser.

quiz.q: Order the first steps for a client reaching a protected remote MCP server.
items: Send a request with no token
Fetch protected resource metadata and read `authorization_servers`
Fetch authorization server metadata (RFC 8414 or OIDC)
Authorize with PKCE `S256` and the `resource` parameter
quiz.explain: The 401 points to protected resource metadata, which names the authorization servers. The client then reads their metadata and only then runs the authorization code flow with PKCE and the resource indicator.

quiz.q: Authorization server metadata does not list `code_challenge_methods_supported`. What must the client do?
options: Fall back to the implicit flow
quiz.explain: Clients MUST use PKCE with S256 and MUST refuse to proceed if the metadata lacks `code_challenge_methods_supported`. Skipping PKCE, using plain or the implicit flow all weaken code protection.

flashcards.front: What order should clients try for registration?
flashcards.back: Pre-registered credentials, then Client ID Metadata Documents, then Dynamic Client Registration (Deprecated), then ask the user.
It names the MCP server (canonical URI, RFC 8707) so the token is audience-bound. Servers MUST validate that tokens were issued for them.

flashcards.front: How does a client find the authorization server?
flashcards.back: Through RFC 9728 protected resource metadata, from `resource_metadata` in the 401 `WWW-Authenticate` header or the well-known URI.
